transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Start: 16:30 PT
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Riya Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Pearl Ops CTO), Sofia Alvarez (PM), Devon Ng (Lead ML Eng)

Summary:
Pearl Ops is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted + dedicated options; they care about time-to-first-token for a PLG quickstart for internal devs, free credits for experimentation, and later possibility of Dedicated or Private (VPC) for PII-sensitive logs. Action items: send quickstart + credits, provision keys, schedule deep dive/benchmark.

Topics:
- Quickstart / time-to-first-token / credits
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC, KMS, SOC2)
- Performance tradeoffs: latency vs cost, batching, KV cache
- Next steps for pilot and benchmarks

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, hey Marcus, Sofia, Devon, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account, with Riya our solutions engineer. How's everybody doing?
[00:00:08] Marcus: Doing well, thanks. Quick at a high level we want to get our product team to try Redwood quickly, see how fast we can go from signup to first token. So time-to-first-token is a big metric for us.
[00:00:18] Riya: great, that's exactly what the quickstart is built for, we usually get devs up in minutes. We also include free credits to make experimenting easier. Can you say a bit about your stack today?
[00:00:27] Sofia: Sure, we currently use OpenAI for most user-facing features. For some internal tooling we've run models on GCP Vertex. We're evaluating alternatives for cost predictability and potential private deployment in future.
[00:00:36] Devon: tech details — we're a mixture of python backends, contouring requests through our API gateway, QPS right now is low, maybe 20 requests/sec peak for dev experiments, prompts average 400 tokens, some longer ones 1.2k.
[00:00:48] Jordan: that's helpful. So hosted Redwood API should be a simple swap in for quick experiments. We have SDKs and a REST endpoint; free credits get you started, then you can pick hosted for PLG or reserve Dedicated if you need predictable throughput and isolation.
[00:00:59] Marcus: How quick is the quickstart? Like can a new engineer get a token and make a request in under an hour?
[00:01:05] Riya: yes, typical path: signup, create API key in console, run the sample app we send — under 10 minutes if you follow the quickstart. There are sometimes hiccups if org SSO is required but for dev accounts it's straightforward. We'll send a link to a repo and a curl example.
[00:01:20] Sofia: And the credits — how do those work? Are there limits and how long do they last?
[00:01:24] Jordan: we provide trial credits tied to the account, usually 30 days, with a quota so teams can't accidentally run up huge bills. For pilots we can extend or move to a paid sandbox.
[00:01:34] Devon: On the security front we need to know about data residency and encryption at rest, KMS integration. Also audit logs — our compliance team will ask for SOC2 and detailed access logs.
[00:01:44] Riya: Redwood is SOC2 compliant; for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and VPC options, plus full audit logs and RBAC. For Hosted we provide enterprise controls like SSO/SAML, encryption at rest, and audit trails. I can share our security pack after the call.
[00:01:56] Marcus: good. Another constraint is latency — our user features are latency sensitive. How does Redwood handle low-latency inference vs cost?
[00:02:04] Riya: couple of levers: Dedicated GPU pools for predictable latency and throughput, and routing policies that prefer lower-latency regions or model variants. We also do intelligent batching and KV cache to reduce tokens per request. For super low latency we recommend Dedicated with pinned models and higher-priority lanes.
[00:02:20] Marcus: okay, can we run a quick benchmark? e.g., a 400-token prompt, measure p50/p95?
[00:02:25] Riya: yes, we usually run a baseline with our sample harness. If you can share representative prompts and QPS we can reproduce latency numbers and advise on model/quantization choices.
[00:02:34] Devon: we'll share prompt templates and current traffic profile, that's part of the action items.
[00:02:37] Jordan: great, that helps. One thing to note: hosted is fastest to get started for devs, but if later you want private data control or compliance, Dedicated or Private can be provisioned — migrations are supported and we support pinning model versions during rollouts.
[00:02:50] Sofia: How often do customers move from hosted to Dedicated? What's the trigger?
[00:02:54] Jordan: common triggers are sustained QPS/cost targets, need for guaranteed capacity (SLA), or strict data controls. Sometimes it's a staged path: start hosted for PLG, then when usage hits a threshold we discuss Dedicated commitments.
[00:03:06] Marcus: pricing model — is hosted usage-based, and Dedicated is reserved capacity?
[00:03:10] Jordan: yes. Hosted is per-token/embedding usage. Dedicated is a reserved GPU pool with monthly or annual commits. We can share a pricing sheet; also we can show cost implications of batching and quantization in the Optimize toolkit.
[00:03:22] Devon: Any gotchas with our infra? We run inside GCP and have a VPC — if we go Private, can Redwood integrate with our network?
[00:03:29] Riya: Private supports VPC peering and on-prem packages for air-gapped needs. For customer-managed keys you'd supply the KMS access; we provide deployment templates for GCP.
[00:03:39] Sofia: competitor question — we use OpenAI for conv features, but cost is creeping up. How would Redwood compare in terms of feature parity?
[00:03:46] Jordan: we support standard text generation, chat, embeddings, and tool-calling primitives; we also publish performance profiles for models and have structured output support. Differences often come down to model catalog and cost/latency tradeoffs. Some customers appreciate Redwood's deployment flexibility and cost controls.
[00:03:59] Marcus: any rough numbers — like per-token delta vs OpenAI?
[00:04:03] Jordan: it varies by model. We'll include some benchmark numbers in the docs we send; also Riya can run a direct cost/latency comparison once we have your samples.
[00:04:11] Speaker 1 (brief interjection): uh I had one question about KV cache — is that something you configure per-route?
[00:04:16] Riya: yes, caching is workload-aware; we can configure prefix/KV cache per-route to speed up repeated context. Sorry sometimes the auto transcript says KV "cash" — it's cache.
[00:04:25] Devon: thanks, small thing — do you support function calling / structured outputs? We rely on structured JSON outputs for downstream parsing.
[00:04:31] Riya: absolutely, we support function/tool calling and structured output. We also have tracing hooks in the console for debugging model outputs.
[00:04:38] Marcus: timeline — we want to enable a small pilot in the next 2–3 weeks if possible. Is that realistic?
[00:04:43] Jordan: totally realistic. Steps would be: 1) we send quickstart + credits, 2) you onboard a few engineers to try the sample app, 3) schedule a benchmark deep dive with Riya and Devon. We can have keys provisioned within 24–48 hours.
[00:04:57] Sofia: who signs off on the pilot internally here? I'll own the PM side, Marcus will own technical sign-off, Devon will run the benchmarks.
[00:05:05] Marcus: yes that works.
[00:05:07] Riya: I'll also include a short checklist for security folks — SOC2 cert, data retention options, KMS steps, and audit log samples.
[00:05:15] Jordan: perfect. Any other concerns before we wrap?
[00:05:18] Devon: just one last thing — sequence lengths up to 1.2k can change perf; when you run the benchmark please include that distribution.
[00:05:25] Riya: noted. We'll run both 400 and 1.2k prompt sets.
[00:05:28] Jordan: awesome. Recap: Jordan sends quickstart + credits + pricing; Riya provisions trial keys and security pack; Devon shares prompts and QPS. Schedule deep dive for next week.
[00:05:40] Marcus: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[00:05:42] Sofia: thank you.
[00:05:44] Jordan: thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invites and links.

End of meeting.
